title: Second frontier lab reaches first-party GA on hyperscaler silicon by Q2 2027
body: Claude's June 29 move to general availability inside Microsoft Foundry — Opus 4.8 and Haiku 4.5 served end-to-end on Azure-hosted NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 systems inside the customer's tenant, under their identity, networking, billing and a single consolidated Azure invoice — sets the template the rest of the PaaS-LLM layer will copy. The deployment shape that matters is 'frontier model, hyperscaler's own silicon, customer tenant, one invoice,' and once one cloud proves enterprises will pay for it, the competitive forcing function is parity: a rival hyperscaler cannot leave its catalog as third-party-API-only while Azure offers in-tenant GA with MEA integration. Expect a second frontier lab to reach equivalent first-party general availability — flagship models running on the hyperscaler's own infrastructure inside the enterprise tenant, not a hosted passthrough — on a competing cloud (Google Cloud Vertex AI on TPU/Blackwell or AWS Bedrock on Trainium/GB300), with consolidated cloud-native billing and the same identity/governance controls, by Q2 2027. The structural pull is that enterprises now treat 'runs in my tenant on the cloud's own hardware' as the procurement bar, turning the PaaS-LLM layer into a multi-cloud parity race rather than an API-access differentiator.

summary: Claude reaching general availability inside Microsoft Foundry on Azure's own GB300 silicon and customer tenant sets a deployment template rivals must match. Competitive parity pressure should push a second frontier lab to equivalent first-party in-tenant GA on Google Cloud or AWS hardware, with consolidated cloud-native billing, by Q2 2027.
